name: Dark Chocolate
description: Fermented and roasted cacao. One of the most chemically complex ingredients you'll find in any kitchen — over 600 volatile compounds.

name: Coffee
description: Roasted seeds of the Coffea plant. The roasting process creates hundreds of aromatic compounds, many of which it shares with chocolate.

name: Vanilla
description: The cured seed pod of a tropical orchid. Vanillin is its signature compound, but the real complexity comes from dozens of supporting molecules.

name: Caramel
description: Browned sugar — the Maillard reaction and caramelization in one. Produces furans, lactones, and diacetyl in abundance.

name: Miso
description: Fermented soybean paste from Japan. The long fermentation creates both savory glutamates and roasted pyrazines — a remarkable depth.

name: Parmesan
description: Aged Italian hard cheese. The two-year aging process concentrates glutamates to near-umami-bomb levels, plus a buttery lactone richness.

name: Black Truffle
description: The most expensive mushroom in the world. Its distinctive aroma comes from dimethyl sulfide and androstenol — unique in the food world.

name: Shiitake Mushroom
description: Dried shiitake is essentially an umami bomb. The drying process concentrates both glutamates and the distinctive mushroom aroma compound 1-octen-3-ol.

name: Cardamom
description: The 'queen of spices.' A warm, eucalyptus-meets-citrus aroma that works equally well in sweet and savory dishes.

name: Lemon
description: Limonene is the star, but lemon's complexity comes from a mix of terpenes, aldehydes, and esters that shift when the zest is heated.

name: Lavender
description: Linalool and linalyl acetate define the lavender aroma. It shares these compounds with bergamot, cardamom, and surprisingly — coriander.

name: Rose
description: Geraniol and citronellol give rose its distinctive scent. A small amount in a dish reads as 'mysterious' rather than 'perfume'.

name: Butter
description: Diacetyl is what makes butter smell buttery. Lactones add a warm, creamy roundness. Fat also carries and amplifies other flavors nearby.

name: Heavy Cream
description: Similar compound profile to butter, but milder. Lactones make it smell faintly of coconut and vanilla — useful bridge ingredient.

name: Strawberry
description: Furaneol is responsible for the candy-sweet top note. Underneath are esters and a touch of linalool that keep it from being one-dimensional.

name: Banana
description: Isoamyl acetate is the banana ester — it's also what gives banana-flavored candy its artificial quality. Natural bananas have eugenol too, which bridges to spices.

name: Pineapple
description: Fruity esters (ethyl butanoate, methyl butanoate) plus furaneol. That's why pineapple works in fermented and caramelized contexts.

name: Dark Rum
description: Distilled fermented sugarcane with barrel aging. Esters from fermentation plus vanillin from the oak — a natural bridge between fruity and caramel.

name: Cinnamon
description: Cinnamaldehyde is the main compound — warm, sweet, slightly peppery. Eugenol connects it to clove and vanilla. Works across almost every category.

name: Clove
description: The most eugenol-dense spice. That's also the compound in vanilla, cinnamon, and basil — clove just has it at overwhelming concentration.

name: Soy Sauce
description: Fermented for 6–18 months. Like miso, it develops both glutamates (savory) and pyrazines (roasted) — but in liquid form.

name: Anchovy
description: Salted and fermented. The result is a concentrated umami hit from glutamates. Dissolves into sauces invisibly but makes everything taste more like itself.

name: Honey
description: Floral volatiles from the bees' plant sources persist in the honey. Furaneol, linalool, and geraniol — it bridges floral, fruity, and sweet categories at once.

name: Smoked Paprika
description: Dried and smoked red peppers. The smoking adds guaiacol and phenol (also in whisky and lapsang) — a bridge between the spice rack and the smokehouse.

name: Mezcal
description: Unlike tequila, mezcal is cooked in underground pits — which gives it guaiacol and phenolic smoke compounds alongside fruity fermentation esters.

name: Beetroot
description: Geosmin gives it that distinctive earthy, just-rained smell. Glutamates add savory depth. Roasting transforms it completely — the geosmin softens and sweetness emerges.

name: Lapsang Souchong
description: Tea smoked over pine wood. Guaiacol dominates — it's essentially liquid smoke in a teacup. Shares smoke compounds with paprika and mezcal.

name: Yuzu
description: Japanese citrus with an aroma unlike anything else — limonene (lemon), nootkatone (grapefruit bitterness), and floral terpenes all at once.

name: Lime
description: Sharper than lemon, with more citral and less sweetness. The zest contains volatile compounds that disappear with heat — always add last.

name: Jasmine
description: Linalool and benzyl acetate define it. Indole — the same compound in jasmine, orange blossom, and certain cheeses — gives it a slightly animal edge that reads as complexity.
